title: Proactive capacity containment and scaleback surge mitigation for dedicated pools
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Summary:
During a customer-facing peak on 2026-03-09 we observed a sustained headroom deficit in two Dedicated GPU pools serving east-us customers. The autoscaler failed to allocate additional shards and in several cases scaled the wrong shard class, which caused a ~30% throughput degradation and transient request queuing for high-priority tenants. This ticket captures the incident timeline, root-cause analysis, immediate mitigations taken, and a prioritized action item list for preventing recurrence.

What happened (concise):
- Time window: 2026-03-09 14:15 - 2026-03-09 17:30 UTC
- Symptom: sustained increase in queue depth and latency, autoscale loop returned fewer shards than required, headroom alarms triggered for multiple pools.
- Impact: degraded throughput for ~8 dedicated customers; automatic fallbacks triggered for 3 customers to lower-capacity model variants. No data loss.

Detection and immediate response: 
- Detection via capacity-slo alert at 14:18 UTC (observability runbook fired).
- Pager to on-call infra and serving teams at 14:21 UTC.
- Quick mitigations: temporarily increased reserve headroom in cluster (14:30 UTC), enabled emergency shard augmentation (14:45 UTC), rolled back autoscaler smoothing parameter patch (15:05 UTC).
- Stabilized baseline throughput by 15:50 UTC; fully recovered to SLOs by 17:20 UTC.

Root cause analysis (summary):
Primary contributors identified: 
1) Autoscaler regression introduced by scheduler refactor (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/core/pull/1197) where the metric-smoothing window default changed from 30s to 5m. This caused the predictive autoscaler to under-react to short sharp increases in QPS, delaying allocation decisions.
2) A secondary mismatch between shard-class selection logic and capacity descriptors (edge-case in pool sizing) caused newly allocated shards to be of a lower throughput SKU in two pools.
3) Monitoring gaps: the headroom prediction alert threshold did not consider the new smoothing behavior, delaying automated remediation triggers.

Why safeguards didn’t stop this: 
- Canary tests exercised long-running steady-state workloads but not short spike scenarios with mixed shard classes.
- Throttle-or-fallback policies were configured but only for hosted tiers; dedicated pools had higher trust and lacked an equivalent fast-fallback policy.

Post-incident impact assessment: 
- Customer-facing latency P99 rose from 120ms to 420ms for affected routes during the incident window.
- Cost delta: emergency augmentation and temporary reserves increased infra spend by ~18% for the day.
- SLA: no SLA breach recorded because fallbacks prevented complete outages, but customer ops received several severity-2 tickets.

Proposed long-term mitigations (high level):
- Reintroduce a spike-detection test harness into the autoscaler canary suite to validate short-duration surges with mixed shard-class constraints.
- Add a fast-fallback headroom policy for Dedicated that mirrors hosted emergency behavior (enable temporary model-variant fallback and cross-pool overflow rules).
- Harden shard-class selection by validating capacity descriptors against expected throughput on allocation path and add pre-allocation unit tests.
- Update alerting thresholds and create a predictive-capacity alarm that factors in smoothing window config.

Links and artifacts: 
- Incident timeline & metrics: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/capacity/incident-2026-03-09
- Related PR (autoscaler smoothing revert): https://github.com/redwood-inference/core/pull/1205
- Scheduler refactor PR for context: https://github.com/redwood-inference/core/pull/1197
- Postmortem draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RES/Dedicated+capacity+2026-03-09+postmortem
